source.title: Train-before-Test Harmonizes Language Model Rankings
source.authors: Guan-Hua Zhang; Ricardo Dominguez-Olmedo; Moritz Hardt

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some figure and table text is flattened, but this does not prevent extracting the reported results below.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests whether held-out corpus perplexity rankings correspond to downstream performance rankings, a different measurement bearing on V6. It does not measure the scaling laws or compute-optimal allocations in the original sources.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. and says benchmark-task exposure can confound scaling laws, but it does not fit or test loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute laws, extrapolate losses, or measure compute-optimal allocations. Rows below cover its reported perplexity-to-downstream ranking correlations for V6. Other ranking-agreement and PCA results do not measure a version of the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well held-out perplexity ranks 53 non-Gemma models against their downstream benchmark ranks, using models from several families on 2025 corpora none of them saw. This bears on V6's 'downstream improves predictably with pretraining loss', through rank correlation rather than fitted curves. It fits no scaling laws, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that, under direct evaluation, the authors find perplexity and downstream rankings largely disconnected (τ=0.48 and 0.55), which they attribute to differing benchmark exposure. They say train-before-test 'restores' the link. For instruction-tuned models they say pre-fine-tuning perplexity does not hold as a predictor, which is stronger than 'weaker'.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares model rankings using benchmark-specific fine-tuning and held-out task evaluation, rather than fitting scaling laws to pretraining loss across parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The perplexity-to-downstream ranking association differs by evaluation scheme (direct evaluation versus train-before-test) and model stage (base versus instruction-tuned).

fits_no_version.finding: Train-before-test raises mean Kendall τ for cross-benchmark ranking agreement from 0.52 to 0.76 (274 of 276 pairs improve). The model×benchmark score matrix becomes nearly rank one, with PC1 explaining 86% of variance (93% within Qwen).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Equalising task-specific fine-tuning makes downstream model rankings consistent across benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: Perplexity rankings agree strongly across the three 2025 corpora: τ=0.76 under direct evaluation and 0.78 after fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Held-out perplexity rankings transfer across text domains.

record.problems: Perplexity agreement experiments exclude Gemma models because the authors report unreliable measurements from the rolling-window implementation. The results are rank correlations rather than fitted loss-scaling curves, and the paper does not report uncertainty for the aggregate Kendall's τ values quoted here.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for claim versions V1–V5 or V7: the reported benchmark ranking agreement, PCA, and compute alignment results do not test those versions. Other perplexity-only corpus-to-corpus agreement results do not measure downstream predictability.

untested.parts: No quantitative fit of downstream score against loss or scale, and no prediction of a specific model's score. Only rank correlations within a cross-section of existing models are reported. Scale is related to downstream performance only qualitatively, through PC1 versus compute.

missing.what: PC1 of train-before-test scores correlates positively with pretraining compute (6ND) across models with known token counts. This bears on V6 via scale; it is qualitative only, with no correlation value given.
Per-corpus results for instruction-tuned models: StackExchange τ values (about 0.26–0.55) are clearly lower than those for Wiki and arXiv.
Separate rows needed for direct-evaluation perplexity–downstream agreement (0.48, 0.55) and for post-fine-tuning perplexity agreement (0.74, 0.84).

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is cross-sectional rank correlations over existing open models up to 14B, with no controlled scaling sweep. The train-before-test perplexity is measured after fine-tuning on the corpora, so it is not pretraining loss in V6's sense. All eight Gemma models are excluded from the perplexity analyses. No uncertainty is reported on the aggregate perplexity τ values. The record's peer-review field ('ICLR 2025') is not supported by the text, which is an arXiv v2 dated October 2025.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss curves versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No power-law fits on small runs or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or comparison of parameter and token scaling.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests across modalities or the listed alternative training regimes.
Tests rank association between held-out corpus perplexity and downstream scores, not a fitted quantitative scaling curve or prediction of task scores from a specified pretraining loss value.
No analysis of scaling-law exponents, fitting choices, or curves bending away from power laws.

rows.subject: 61 language models (aggregate; Gemma models excluded from perplexity agreement experiments)
rows.size_stated: Models selected with no more than 14B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared average Kendall's τ between perplexity rankings on three 2025 corpora and downstream benchmark rankings across evaluation schemes.
rows.measure: Average Kendall's τ between perplexity rankings and downstream benchmark rankings
rows.note: Aggregate ranking correlations across the evaluated models, three perplexity corpora, and 24 downstream benchmarks.
rows.check: Two conditions are merged into one row. Only the direct-evaluation baseline (mean τ=0.48, which the authors call low, a 'disconnect') compares pretraining-loss perplexity with downstream scores. The train-before-test value (0.74) uses perplexity after fine-tuning on the corpora's train splits, so it is not pretraining loss. Split into two rows. The subject should be 53 models, not 61: all 8 Gemma models are excluded (Table 3), although the text says 'four'.

source_check.correct: Perplexity experiments exclude eight Gemma models, leaving 53 of the 61 models. Direct evaluation compares pre-task-fine-tuning perplexity and downstream rankings: mean Kendall τ=0.48, partial for V6. Train-before-test compares post-fine-tuning perplexity and downstream rankings: mean τ=0.74; this value does not directly measure predictability from pretraining loss. Separate these conditions rather than assigning one V6 state.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, Figure 4 and caption; Introduction Section 1.1; Appendix B.2 and Table 3.
source_check.problem: The model count is wrong, and the row merges pre- and post-fine-tuning loss comparisons under one V6 state.

rows.subject: 61 language models (aggregate; Gemma models excluded from perplexity agreement experiments)
rows.size_stated: Models selected with no more than 14B parameters
rows.operation_detail: Compared the ranking by average perplexity across the three corpora with the ranking by average downstream performance across the benchmarks.
rows.measure: Kendall's τ between average perplexity ranking and average downstream performance ranking
rows.note: Aggregate correlation reported separately from the mean correlation across individual benchmark rankings in R1.
rows.check: Same issue as R1. The direct-evaluation τ=0.55, which the authors call 'modest', is the pretraining-loss measure. The train-before-test 0.84 uses post-fine-tuning perplexity. The subject excludes all 8 Gemma models (53 models remain).

source_check.correct: The perplexity experiment covers 53 non-Gemma models. Kendall τ between average perplexity ranking and average downstream ranking is 0.55 under direct evaluation and 0.84 under train-before-test. The latter uses post-fine-tuning perplexity. Separate the direct-evaluation V6 result, partial, from the post-fine-tuning comparison, which cannot determine predictability from pretraining loss.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3, paragraphs spanning pages 9–10; Figure 5 caption distinguishes the evaluation schemes; Appendix B.2 and Table 3.
source_check.problem: The model count is wrong, and the reported improvement changes both perplexity and downstream evaluation stages.

rows.note: Aggregate result; the authors describe this association as substantially weaker than for base models.

relationships.condition: Base models; pre-fine-tuning perplexity versus downstream rank after task fine-tuning
relationships.reason: Pre-fine-tuning perplexity ranks agree strongly with post-fine-tuning downstream ranks, mean Kendall τ=0.78 (R3).
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity rankings before fine-tuning agreed strongly with downstream rankings afterward, with mean Kendall τ=0.78.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Base models; pre-fine-tuning perplexity versus downstream rank after task fine-tuning
source_check.reason: R3 reports strong ranking agreement, mean Kendall τ=0.78, for non-Gemma base models. This supports ranking predictability in the tested adaptation setting.

relationships.condition: Direct (out-of-the-box) evaluation across model families with different pretraining data
relationships.reason: Pretraining perplexity agrees only weakly with direct downstream ranks: mean τ=0.48 per benchmark (R1) and τ=0.55 on the average score (R2). The authors attribute this to differing benchmark exposure across families.
relationships.display_finding: Pretraining perplexity had mean rank agreement τ=0.48 per benchmark and τ=0.55 for average downstream scores, which the authors attributed to differing benchmark exposure.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Direct (out-of-the-box) evaluation across model families with different pretraining data
source_check.reason: The direct-evaluation portions of R1 and R2 report low or modest agreement, τ=0.48 and 0.55. These positive but incomplete associations qualify downstream predictability across heterogeneous training histories; differing benchmark exposure is the authors' hypothesis.

relationships.reason: Perplexity before fine-tuning tracks downstream ranks after fine-tuning much less, τ=0.51 (R4). The authors say instruction tuning makes perplexity rankings unreliable.
relationships.display_finding: Perplexity measured after instruction tuning had only τ=0.51 agreement with downstream rankings.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: R4 measures perplexity after instruction tuning, not pretraining loss, and supplies no scale-based predictability test. Its τ=0.51 establishes unreliable rankings from instruction-tuned-model perplexity, but does not directly test the stated V6 predictor.
